name: Mobile Security
description: Security and privacy of Android and iOS apps, permissions, app stores, and mobile platforms.

ccs.narrative:
Research on mobile security at CCS began taking shape around 2018, with early work concentrating on mobile OS security, app analysis, and smartphone privacy. JN-SAF: Precise and Efficient NDK/JNI-aware Inter-language Static Analysis Framework for Security Vetting of Android Applications with Native Code (CCS 2018) set an influential baseline by showing how to Inter-language static analysis framework vetting Android apps that mix Java and native NDK/JNI code. Parallel contributions—The Web's Sixth Sense: A Study of Scripts Accessing Smartphone Sensors (2018) and PatternListener: Cracking Android Pattern Lock Using Acoustic Signals (2018) —reinforced the foundational challenges in this space.

A productive wave of CCS work from 2020–2022 deepened the area. Enhancing State-of-the-art Classifiers with API Semantics to Detect Evolved Android Malware (CCS 2020) advanced the field by demonstrating Enhances Android malware classifiers with API semantics to resist performance aging from evolving malware. Other strong contributions included Consistency Analysis of Data-Usage Purposes in Mobile Apps (2021), EchoHand: High Accuracy and Presentation Attack Resistant Hand Authentication on Commodity Mobile Devices (2022), broadening the space of techniques and targets.

The most recent CCS contributions (from 2023 onward) reflect a maturing field that pushes into harder targets and broader threat models. Recovering Fingerprints from In-Display Fingerprint Sensors via Electromagnetic Side Channel (CCS 2023) exemplified this trend by tackling Reconstructs user fingerprints from in-display sensors by capturing electromagnetic side-channel emissions during.... Similarly, Don't Leak Your Keys: Understanding, Measuring, and Exploiting the AppSecret Leaks in Mini-Programs (2023) and PolicyChecker: Analyzing the GDPR Completeness of Mobile Apps' Privacy Policies (2023) show how the community continues to scale and adapt its methods.

uss.narrative:
The earliest listed work, from USENIX Security 2018, reflects a field maturing along two tracks: deep platform and analysis tooling, and privacy. On the systems side, "Charm: Facilitating Dynamic Analysis of Device Drivers of Mobile Systems" (USENIX 2018) and "ATtention Spanned: Comprehensive Vulnerability Analysis of AT Commands Within the Android Ecosystem" (USENIX 2018) pushed analysis down into drivers and modem interfaces, while "Tackling runtime-based obfuscation in Android with TIRO" (USENIX 2018) confronted malware that actively hid from analysis. In parallel, "FlowCog: Context-aware Semantics Extraction and Analysis of Information Flow Leaks in Android Apps" (USENIX 2018) and the meta-study "Discovering Flaws in Security-Focused Static Analysis Tools for Android using Systematic Mutation" (USENIX 2018) showed both the promise and the fragility of the static-analysis toolchain the community had come to rely on.

The next shift, around 2019-2020, was a turn toward privacy policy and data-flow accountability at app-store scale. "PolicyLint: Investigating Internal Privacy Policy Contradictions on Google Play" (USENIX 2019) introduced automated reasoning over the gap between what apps say and do, and "Actions Speak Louder than Words: Entity-Sensitive Privacy Policy and Data Flow Analysis with PoliCheck" (USENIX 2020) extended this to entity-sensitive flow checking, becoming a heavily cited anchor for policy-compliance research. The same period broadened the platform attack surface dramatically: "FIRMSCOPE" (USENIX 2020) mined pre-installed firmware apps for privilege escalation, "PARTEMU" (USENIX 2020) opened TrustZone software to dynamic analysis, and "FANS" (USENIX 2020) fuzzed Android native system services, signaling that vendor firmware, secure-world code, and system services were now first-class targets.

By 2021-2022 the area diversified into ecosystem and human-factors questions alongside novel side channels. Work like "An Investigation of the Android Kernel Patch Ecosystem" (USENIX 2021) and "Why Eve and Mallory Still Love Android: Revisiting TLS (In)Security in Android Applications" (USENIX 2021) revisited whether years of attention had actually fixed patching and TLS validation, while "A Large Scale Study of User Behavior, Expectations and Engagement with Android Permissions" (USENIX 2021) centered real users across countries. New attack classes appeared in third-party libraries ("Understanding Malicious Cross-library Data Harvesting on Android", USENIX 2021), app-in-app super-app ecosystems ("Identity Confusion in WebView-based Mobile App-in-app Ecosystems", USENIX 2022), and physical side channels ("Charger-Surfing", USENIX 2021). Voice assistants also became a recurring theme, from "SkillExplorer" (USENIX 2020) to "SkillDetective" (USENIX 2022).

Most recently, in 2023, the field is wrestling with machine learning robustness and entirely new sensing modalities. "Continuous Learning for Android Malware Detection" (USENIX 2023) tackles concept drift that erodes ML malware classifiers over time, a sign that detection itself is now a moving target. Meanwhile the definition of a mobile platform keeps expanding: "Going through the motions: AR/VR keylogging from user head motions" (USENIX 2023) treats AR/VR headsets as the next mobile frontier, and "Eavesdropping Mobile App Activity via Radio-Frequency Energy Harvesting" (USENIX 2023) shows app activity leaking through ambient RF, pushing mobile security well beyond the classic phone-app threat model.
